questions.q: In a 1-D launch, what is the usual global index of a thread?
options: `blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x`
`threadIdx.x * gridDim.x + blockIdx.x`
`blockIdx.x + threadIdx.x`
`blockDim.x * gridDim.x`
questions.why: Each block covers `blockDim.x` consecutive elements, so block b starts at b·blockDim.x and the thread adds its offset within the block.

questions.q: You launch 256 threads per block for n = 1000 elements. How many blocks do you need, and what must the kernel check?
options: 4 blocks, and each thread must check `i <= n`
1000 blocks of one thread each
4 blocks, and each thread must check `i < n` before touching memory
3 blocks, with no check
questions.why: ceil(1000/256) = 4 gives 1024 threads. The last 24 would read and write out of bounds without the guard.

questions.q: What is a grid-stride loop?
options: A loop over the blocks inside one thread
A recursive kernel launch
A loop where each thread handles elements i, i + stride, i + 2·stride, ... with stride = total threads in the grid
A loop that synchronises all blocks each iteration
questions.why: It lets a fixed-size launch process any n and keeps accesses coalesced, since neighbouring threads still touch neighbouring elements.

questions.q: Why should block sizes usually be a multiple of 32?
options: Shared memory only works in multiples of 32
Threads execute in warps of 32, so other sizes leave lanes idle in the last warp
It makes integer division exact
The hardware rejects other sizes
questions.why: A block of 100 threads uses 4 warps (128 lanes), wasting 28.

questions.q: What is warp divergence?
options: Two warps writing the same address
Blocks finishing in a different order
Different kernels running at once
Threads of one warp taking different branches, so the paths run one after another with some lanes masked off
questions.why: An element-wise `if x > 0` usually costs little, since both paths are short. Divergence hurts most when branches are long and data-dependent.

questions.q: A GELU kernel uses `tanhf` and `expf`. Why are element-wise activation kernels usually memory-bound?
options: They do a few arithmetic operations per element but must read and write every element from global memory
Each thread runs a loop over the whole array
Transcendental functions run on the CPU
They need many synchronisations
questions.why: The GPU can do far more arithmetic per second than it can move bytes. Fusing an activation into the kernel that produces its input avoids a full extra read and write.

questions.q: Which numerically safe form of sigmoid avoids overflow for large negative x?
options: Always `1 / (1 + expf(-x))`
`expf(x) / expf(x + 1)`
`x / (1 + fabsf(x))`
For x < 0, compute `e / (1 + e)` with `e = expf(x)`; for x ≥ 0, compute `1 / (1 + expf(-x))`
questions.why: `expf(-x)` overflows to infinity for x around -89 in float32. Choosing the form by sign keeps every exponent's argument ≤ 0.

questions.q: A kernel launch returns immediately. How do you make sure it finished and check for errors?
options: Read the output array; that always waits
Call `cudaDeviceSynchronize()` (or synchronise a stream) and check `cudaGetLastError()`
The launch blocks until done
Errors are printed automatically
questions.why: Launches are asynchronous. Launch-configuration errors show up from `cudaGetLastError`; errors during execution show up at the next synchronising call.

questions.q: In a 2-D launch over an M×N row-major matrix, why is `threadIdx.x` usually mapped to the column?
options: Columns are always shorter
Consecutive threads in a warp then read consecutive addresses, so loads coalesce
`threadIdx.y` can't exceed 1
Row-major matrices are stored by column
questions.why: In row-major storage, element (r, c) is at r·N + c. Neighbouring c values are neighbouring addresses.

questions.q: Why is a naive matrix transpose slow?
options: Either the reads or the writes are strided by the row length, so one side doesn't coalesce
It needs atomics
Transposition needs floating-point arithmetic
It can only use one block
questions.why: The fix is to load a tile into shared memory with coalesced reads, then write it out transposed, also coalesced. Padding the tile to 33 columns avoids bank conflicts.

questions.q: In a naive matmul kernel computing one C element per thread, how many global loads does each thread do for K = 1024?
options: About 2048: one row of A and one column of B
questions.why: Every thread rereads data its neighbours also read. Tiling into shared memory reuses each loaded value across a whole tile of threads.

questions.q: The outer product of vectors u (length M) and v (length N) is computed with one thread per output. What is its arithmetic intensity like?
options: Unbounded
Higher than matmul
Very low: one multiply per output element written
Zero, since no memory is used
questions.why: It writes M·N values but does only M·N multiplies, so it is bound by write bandwidth.

questions.q: For a row-wise LayerNorm kernel, a common mapping is one block per row. Why?
options: Blocks can't access columns
Rows are always 32 wide
The mean and variance need a reduction over the row, which threads in a block can do through shared memory
It avoids any synchronisation
questions.why: Threads cooperate on the row's sum and sum of squares, synchronise, then each normalises its own elements.

questions.q: What does RMSNorm skip compared with LayerNorm?
options: Subtracting the mean, and usually the bias
The square root
The learned scale
The division
questions.why: RMSNorm computes $x/\sqrt{\text{mean}(x^2) + \epsilon} \cdot g$. One reduction instead of two passes makes the kernel simpler and cheaper.

questions.q: For matrix-vector multiply y = A x with A row-major, which mapping gives coalesced reads of A?
options: One thread per column
One thread per row reading the whole row alone
One warp per row, with lanes striding across the row's columns and a warp reduction at the end
One block per element of A
questions.why: With one thread per row, neighbouring threads read addresses a full row apart. Warp-per-row reads contiguous memory and reduces with shuffles.

questions.q: Why do 2-D kernels need bounds checks on both indices?
options: Only the y index can overflow
The grid is rounded up in both dimensions, so edge blocks have threads past the last row or column
Threads can have negative indices
Shared memory is two-dimensional
questions.why: A 100×100 matrix with 16×16 blocks uses a 7×7 grid covering 112×112, so threads must check `r < M && c < N`.

questions.q: In a tree reduction within a block, why is `__syncthreads()` needed between steps?
options: To start the next kernel
Each step reads values written by other threads in the previous step
To allocate shared memory
To flush the L2 cache
questions.why: Without the barrier, a thread may read a partial sum before its partner has written it.

questions.q: Why is `if (tid % (2*s) == 0)` a poor indexing scheme for a reduction?
options: It uses too much shared memory
It gives the wrong answer
It doesn't terminate
Active threads are scattered across warps, causing divergence in every warp
questions.why: Using `if (tid < s)` with a halving stride keeps active threads contiguous, so whole warps retire early.

questions.q: What do warp shuffle instructions like `__shfl_down_sync` let you do?
options: Move data between blocks
Reorder global memory
Synchronise the whole grid
Exchange registers between lanes of a warp without going through shared memory
questions.why: The last five steps of a reduction can run with shuffles, cutting shared-memory traffic and barriers.

questions.q: How do you combine per-block partial sums into a single total?
options: Read them on the device in the first kernel without synchronisation
Launch a second small reduction kernel, or have each block do one `atomicAdd` into the result
Use `__syncthreads()` across blocks
Each block writes to the same address without atomics
questions.why: Blocks can't synchronise with each other within a normal launch. Atomics are simplest; a second pass is deterministic.

questions.q: Why can a float sum computed on the GPU differ slightly between runs or from the CPU?
options: Memory corruption
The CPU rounds differently for every value
Floating-point addition isn't associative, and the order of additions differs
GPUs use lower precision for all sums
questions.why: Atomics complete in a nondeterministic order. Fixed-order tree reductions are reproducible run to run but still differ from a sequential sum.

questions.q: How is mean and variance computed in one pass without catastrophic cancellation?
options: Welford's algorithm, merging (count, mean, M2) triples in the reduction
Two separate kernels that each read the data twice
Sum x and x² and use E[x²] - E[x]²
Compute the median first
questions.why: E[x²] - E[x]² subtracts two nearly equal numbers when the mean is large compared with the spread. Welford partials combine with a closed-form merge.

questions.q: For argmax, what must each reduction step carry?
options: The sum of the values
Only the index
Only the value
Both the value and its index, with a fixed tie-breaking rule
questions.why: Comparing values alone loses the position. Breaking ties by the smaller index gives the same answer as a sequential scan.

questions.q: What should a max reduction use as the identity for threads past the end of the array?
options: Negative infinity (`-INFINITY`)
Zero
The first element of the array always
One
questions.why: Zero is wrong when every value is negative. The identity must not change the result when combined with any real value.

questions.q: In a 1-D convolution kernel with filter width K, why stage input into shared memory?
options: To avoid bounds checks
Shared memory is larger than global memory
Neighbouring outputs share K - 1 inputs, so a block loads its tile plus a halo once and reuses it
Global memory can't be read inside a loop
questions.why: Without staging, each input element is read K times from global memory.

questions.q: What is the halo of a tile in a stencil kernel?
options: The extra border elements beyond the tile that its outputs need
The padding added to the final result
The output region
Unused threads
questions.why: For a 3×3 filter, a 16×16 output tile needs an 18×18 input tile.

questions.q: Where should a small convolution filter be stored when every thread reads the same weights?
options: Texture memory written by each thread
Constant memory, which broadcasts a value to all threads that read it together
A separate global array per block
Local memory
questions.why: Constant memory is cached and optimised for warp-uniform reads, which is exactly the filter access pattern.

questions.q: A 2-D convolution over C_in channels to C_out channels at H×W output with a k×k kernel does how many multiply-adds?
options: $H \cdot W \cdot C_{out} \cdot C_{in} \cdot k^2$
$C_{in} \cdot C_{out}$
$H \cdot W \cdot (C_{in} + C_{out})$
$H \cdot W \cdot k^2$
questions.why: Each output value sums over all input channels and kernel taps. Large convolutions are usually lowered to matmul (im2col or implicit GEMM).

questions.q: What does im2col do?
options: Converts the image to grayscale
Transposes the filter
Unrolls every receptive-field patch into a column, so the convolution becomes one matrix multiply
Compresses the input
questions.why: It costs extra memory (k² copies of the input) but uses a highly optimised GEMM.

questions.q: A 3-D convolution has a larger halo per tile than a 2-D one. Why does that hurt more?
options: Halos don't exist in 3-D
3-D tensors can't use shared memory
3-D needs more registers per output only
The halo grows in three dimensions, so a larger fraction of each tile is reloaded overlap
questions.why: For an 8³ output tile with a 3³ filter, the input tile is 10³ = 1000 values for 512 outputs.

questions.q: How is max pooling with a 2×2 window and stride 2 typically mapped to threads?
options: One warp per input row with no output mapping
One block per image doing a full sort
One thread per input element writing with atomics
One thread per output element, reading its four inputs
questions.why: With no overlap between windows, each output is independent and the reads are mostly coalesced.

questions.q: How should a convolution handle "same" padding at image borders?
options: Read whatever is in memory there
Treat out-of-range input coordinates as zero (or the chosen padding value) when loading
Skip the border outputs entirely
Wrap around to the opposite edge by default
questions.why: Bounds checks when loading the tile and halo replace out-of-range reads with the padding value.

questions.q: Why compute cross-entropy from logits using log-sum-exp rather than softmax followed by log?
options: It is the only differentiable form
It needs no reduction
It avoids overflow in exp and underflow in log for large or very negative logits
Softmax is undefined for more than two classes
questions.why: $\text{CE} = \log\sum_j e^{z_j - m} + m - z_y$ with $m = \max_j z_j$. Every exponent is ≤ 0.

questions.q: What is fusion in the context of GPU kernels?
options: Combining several operations in one kernel so intermediates stay in registers or shared memory
Compiling CPU and GPU code together
Merging two GPUs
Launching the same kernel twice
questions.why: A softmax followed by a cross-entropy in separate kernels writes and rereads the probability tensor. Fused, it never leaves the chip.

questions.q: In inverted dropout, what happens to kept values during training?
options: They are unchanged, and inference scales by (1 - p)
They are scaled by p
They are set to 1
They are scaled by 1/(1 - p)
questions.why: Scaling at training time keeps the expected activation unchanged, so inference is just the identity.

questions.q: How does a dropout kernel get random numbers on the GPU?
options: By calling `rand()` in each thread
From a counter-based generator such as Philox, keyed by seed and element index
From uninitialised memory
By copying random numbers from the CPU each step
questions.why: Counter-based generators let any thread compute its random number independently and reproducibly, and let the backward pass regenerate the same mask.

questions.q: Scaled dot-product attention divides scores by $\sqrt{d}$. Why?
options: To reduce memory use
Dot products of random d-dimensional vectors have variance growing with d, which would saturate the softmax
It is required for causal masking
To make the scores positive
questions.why: Without scaling, large scores make softmax nearly one-hot and gradients tiny.

questions.q: A naive attention kernel writes the full T×T score matrix to global memory. What is the main cost at long T?
options: Registers overflow for every T
The number of multiply-adds becomes linear
Memory traffic and storage grow with T², dominating runtime
The softmax becomes unstable
questions.why: FlashAttention tiles over keys with an online softmax so scores never leave on-chip memory.

questions.q: For cosine similarity between rows of two matrices, which values must a kernel reduce?
options: Only the norms
The sum of absolute differences
Only the dot product
The dot product and both squared norms, with an ε guard in the division
questions.why: cos = a·b / (‖a‖‖b‖ + ε). All three sums can be accumulated in a single pass over the row.

questions.q: Why do fused kernels often compute in float32 even when inputs are float16?
options: float16 isn't supported on GPUs
float32 uses less memory
Accumulating sums and exponentials in half precision loses accuracy or overflows
It makes the kernel faster in all cases
questions.why: Load in half, accumulate in float, and write back in half. This mixed-precision pattern keeps the bandwidth savings without the error.

questions.q: What is the key idea of tiled matrix multiplication?
options: Tiles are computed in a random order
Each thread computes the whole output
Matrices are split across GPUs
Each block loads tiles of A and B into shared memory once and reuses every loaded value many times
questions.why: With T×T tiles, each global load is used T times, cutting global traffic by a factor of about T.

questions.q: In a shared-memory tiled matmul, why are there two `__syncthreads()` per tile step?
options: One after loading the tile so all values are present, and one after computing so no thread overwrites a tile still being read
They are optional
One per input matrix
One to start and one to end the kernel
questions.why: Without the second barrier, a fast thread could start loading the next tile while slower threads are still reading the current one.

questions.q: What is arithmetic intensity?
options: The number of floating-point operations per byte moved from memory
The number of threads per block
The clock rate of the GPU
The ratio of shared to global memory
questions.why: Kernels below the machine's balance point (peak FLOP/s ÷ bandwidth) are memory-bound; above it, compute-bound.

questions.q: Why does register tiling (each thread computing a small block of outputs) help beyond shared-memory tiling?
options: It reduces the number of blocks to one
Values loaded from shared memory into registers are reused across several outputs, cutting shared-memory traffic
Registers are larger than shared memory
It removes the need for shared memory
questions.why: A thread computing a 4×4 sub-tile reuses each loaded A value 4 times and each B value 4 times.

questions.q: What is occupancy?
options: The ratio of active warps on an SM to the maximum it can hold
The share of time spent in shared memory
The number of kernels running
The fraction of global memory in use
questions.why: Registers per thread, shared memory per block and block size all limit it. Higher occupancy hides latency, but it isn't the only route to speed.

questions.q: Why can a larger tile size reduce performance even though it improves reuse?
options: Tiles must equal the warp size
It needs more shared memory and registers per block, which can lower occupancy or cause spills
Larger tiles give wrong results
Global memory can't serve large tiles
questions.why: Tile size is a trade-off between reuse and how many blocks fit on an SM. Libraries autotune it per shape.

questions.q: When must a tiled matmul pad or guard tile loads?
options: Only when the matrices are square
Only for the output tile
When M, N or K is not a multiple of the tile size; out-of-range elements are loaded as zero
Never; tiles always divide the matrix
questions.why: Zero padding in the K direction leaves the dot products unchanged, and guards on M and N stop stray writes.

questions.q: What hardware feature do modern GPUs offer to accelerate tiled matmul beyond CUDA cores?
options: Warp divergence
Constant memory
Texture units
Tensor cores, which compute small matrix multiply-accumulates per instruction
questions.why: Tensor cores operate on fragments such as 16×16 tiles in reduced precision with higher-precision accumulation, giving several times the FLOP/s.
